seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
title: DSA: interview routine, arrays and hashing
description: The clarify-brute-force-optimise-code-dry-run routine, complexity reasoning, and the hash map / prefix sum toolbox: two sum, subarray sum equals K, group anagrams, top-K frequent.
source: LeetCode problem set and discuss; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; Python docs (collections, heapq); Oracle Java docs (HashMap)

questions.prompt: Match each step of the coding-interview routine with what you do in it.

right.text: Ask about input size, duplicates, negatives and what to return when no answer exists
State a simple correct baseline and its cost, so you always have a fallback
Trace the finished code by hand on a small example, tracking every variable
Try empty, single-element, all-equal and maximum-size inputs
Give time and space in terms of n and name the dominant term
Rewrite the solution in a second language

questions.explanation: The order is clarify, brute force, better idea, code, dry run, test, complexity. Interviewers grade the routine as much as the final code; skipping the brute force and the dry run is the most common way to lose points.

questions.text: First {1} the problem and constraints, then state a {2} solution with its cost, look for a better idea, write the code, and {3} it by hand on a small input before declaring it done.
questions.explanation: Constraints drive the target complexity: n up to 10^5 usually means O(n log n) or better, n up to 20 allows exponential search.

questions.prompt: A brute-force two sum checks every pair i < j in an array of 10 elements. How many pair checks happen in the worst case?
questions.explanation: n(n-1)/2 = 10*9/2 = 45. That quadratic growth is why the brute force is too slow for n = 10^5 (about 5 billion pairs) and why you reach for a hash map.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Sorting an array and then finding a pair with a target sum using two pointers is O(n log n) overall.
questions.reason: The two-pointer scan itself is O(n), but sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates.

whys.a: Correct: the total is the sum of the phases, and the largest term wins.
whys.b: Both are true, but R is exactly why the total is O(n log n), so it does explain A.
whys.c: A is true, so this cannot be the answer.
whys.d: A is true, so this cannot be the answer.

questions.explanation: Add the phases and keep the dominant term: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A HashMap-based two sum is guaranteed O(n) time even in the worst case.
questions.reason: HashMap get and put take O(1) time on average.

whys.a: A is not true as stated, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so option c cannot hold.
whys.d: Correct: O(1) is an average-case (expected) bound. With many collisions Java falls back to tree bins (O(log n) per lookup) and Python dicts can degrade, so the worst case is not O(n).

questions.explanation: Say "expected O(n)" in an interview. It shows you know the difference between expected and worst-case hash costs.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: After one O(n) pass, a prefix-sum array answers any range-sum query in O(1).
questions.reason: Arrays support O(1) random access by index.

whys.a: R is true but it is not the reason: the O(1) comes from prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but the real reason is the subtraction identity, not random access alone.
whys.c: A is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]. The same idea, with a hash map of earlier prefixes, solves "subarray sum equals K".

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Grouping anagrams by the sorted string key costs O(n * k log k) for n words of length k.
questions.reason: Sorting the k characters of one word takes O(k) time.

whys.a: R is false, so this cannot be right.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option holds.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (n sorts of cost k log k) but sorting k characters takes O(k log k), not O(k).
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The alternative key is a 26-count tuple, giving O(n * k) for lowercase words. Mention both.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) that returns the indices of two different elements adding up to target in one pass using a HashMap (assume exactly one answer exists).
questions.starter:
static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
  
}

checks.label: uses a HashMap/Map from value to index
looks up the complement target - nums[i]
checks the map with get or containsKey

questions.explanation: Check the map before inserting the current element, otherwise [3,2,4] with target 6 pairs index 0 with itself. Other correct solutions (containsKey, a fill-first pass) also pass.

questions.prompt: This Python two sum inserts first and then checks: for x in nums: seen[x] = i; if target - x in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]. What does it return for nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6?

options.why: Right: seen[3] = 0 is stored before the lookup of 6 - 3 = 3, so the element matches itself.
The correct answer, but this code never reaches it because it returns on the first element.

options.text: None, because no pair sums to 6
options.why: 2 + 4 = 6 exists; the bug is the order of insert and check.

options.text: It raises KeyError on the first iteration
options.why: The check uses "in", so no KeyError is raised.

questions.explanation: Look up the complement before storing the current value. This is the classic "use the same element twice" bug.

questions.prompt: Python's Counter.most_common(k) is implemented with a heap, so selecting the top k of n distinct keys costs about O(n log k) rather than a full sort.

options.why: Right: for a given k it uses heapq.nlargest; with no argument it sorts everything.
It is not a full sort when k is given; heapq.nlargest keeps a heap of size k.

questions.explanation: Top-K frequent: count with a hash map (O(n)), then use a size-k min-heap (O(n log k)) or bucket sort by frequency (O(n)).

questions.prompt: How many contiguous subarrays of [3, 4, -3, 1, 2, -1, 2] sum to K = 3?
questions.explanation: They are [3], [4,-3,1,2,-1], [1,2] and [2,-1,2]. The prefix-sum map finds them in O(n); because of the negative numbers a sliding window would not work.

questions.text: Keep a running {1} sum; the number of earlier prefixes equal to {2} is how many subarrays end here; seed the map with {3} so subarrays starting at index 0 count.
questions.explanation: Because values can be negative a sliding window does not work (extending the window does not monotonically grow the sum), so prefix sums with a frequency map are the standard answer.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function group_anagrams(strs) that returns the words grouped so that anagrams share a group. Use a dictionary keyed by the sorted letters.

checks.label: uses a dict that groups lists (defaultdict, setdefault or get)
builds a key from the sorted characters
joins or tuples the sorted letters into a hashable key
appends each word to its group

questions.explanation: A list cannot be a dict key, so join or tuple the sorted letters. A tuple of 26 counts also works and is faster for long words.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function longest_consecutive(nums) returning the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like 3,4,5,6) present in an unsorted list, in O(n) expected time using a set.

checks.label: puts the numbers in a set
only starts counting at a number whose predecessor is absent
extends the run with a loop

questions.explanation: Starting only at run beginnings means each element is visited at most twice overall, so it is O(n) expected despite the nested loop. Sorting is O(n log n) and also accepted by interviewers as a first answer, but the question asks for O(n).

questions.prompt: A Java class overrides equals but not hashCode, and instances are stored in a HashSet. What can go wrong?

options.text: Equal objects can land in different buckets, so contains may fail.
options.why: Right: the contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes; otherwise lookup probes the wrong bucket.

options.text: The class fails to compile, because the compiler insists both methods are overridden together.
options.why: The compiler does not enforce the pair; the bug appears at run time as missed lookups.

options.text: The set throws an exception on the second add of an object equal to an existing one.
options.why: HashSet does not throw on duplicates; add just returns false when it finds an equal element.

options.text: The set switches to comparing by identity for every later call to add or contains.
options.why: It still calls equals and hashCode; it just receives inconsistent hash values.

questions.explanation: Also never use a mutable field in hashCode for keys you keep in a map: changing it after insertion loses the entry. Objects.hash(...) and records give a correct pair for free.

questions.prompt: For nums = [2, 3, 4, 5], the product-except-self array has output[i] equal to the product of all other elements. What is output[1]?
questions.explanation: 2 * 4 * 5 = 40. The O(n) solution without division multiplies a running prefix product on the way right and a running suffix product on the way back, using the output array itself, so extra space is O(1) besides the answer.
